title: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, with Shankara's commentary
attributionNote: The Upanishad is anonymous; its central teaching is placed in the mouth of the sage Yajnavalkya at the court of king Janaka, and the text preserves that dialogue rather than claiming a single author. The commentary carried beside the text is ascribed to Shankara.
description: The longest and oldest of the principal Upanishads, the Brihadaranyaka opens with the sacrifice of the horse as a figure of the cosmos and then pursues the self: in Yajnavalkya's answers to his wife Maitreyi and to the assembly at Janaka's court, being is described as the one to be heard, reflected on and known — not this, not this, the self that is the light of every act of knowing. It ends with the prayer to lead the reader from darkness to light.
historicalContext: Its teaching is the basis of the Advaita Vedanta the commentaries elaborate and of much of later Indian thought about consciousness. Shankara's Bhashya is the commentary through which the Upanishad was read in the monastic schools, and the Kanva recension printed here is the one the commentary follows.
availabilityNote: Complete: the six adhyayas of the Kanva recension from the GRETIL e-text, streamed at read time one brahmana at a time, with the commentary ascribed to Shankara in a second pane. Both texts are read from the same GRETIL file under their own reference markers.
